executive_summary: CAD/CHF trades at 0.57412 (5 August close), sitting at the 36th percentile of a 52-week range that runs 0.55955–0.60047 and holding a fractional +0.01% gain over twelve months — making this the quietest major cross in the G10 despite a 225bp policy differential that should, mechanically, have dragged it steadily higher. The provided performance set shows -0.26% over one month, +1.42% over three, -0.02% over six and +0.01% over one year; the daily candles tell a sharper story, with the pair rallying 178 pips from the 5 July low of 0.56448 to a 29 July high of 0.58228 before surrendering 140 pips of that in six sessions. The dominant bilateral narrative is a pure carry-and-policy-inertia trade: the Bank of Canada sits at 2.25% against a Swiss National Bank at 0.00%, a differential that widens to +271bp at the two-year point and +311bp at ten years, and both central banks are the two most policy-static in the G10 — the BoC because core inflation is below target, the SNB because it has published a three-year conditional forecast conditioned on doing nothing at all. Three bilateral differentials diverge materially from what a naive combination of the two dossiers would produce. First, positioning: the CAD dossier flags a twenty-year record speculative short while the CHF dossier finds franc positioning unremarkable, which means the implied pair position is short CAD/CHF and the squeeze asymmetry runs to the upside — a signal absent from both standalone views. Second, trade policy: Canada faces 50% Section 338 tariffs from around 19 August while Switzerland faces 15% capped Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs from 29 September, so the single largest negative in each dossier partially cancels bilaterally. Third, valuation: both dossiers independently imply a CAD/CHF fair value near 0.6100 on relative real effective exchange rates, placing spot 6.1% cheap — the rare configuration in which carry and valuation point the same way. We are Bullish CAD/CHF tactically at conviction 4 (weighted score +0.525, confidence 63%) and Bullish strategically at conviction 3 (+0.300, 59%), with the explicit caveat that this is a positive-carry position in a pair whose downside is doubly convex: a genuine risk-off event weakens the base leg and bids the quote leg simultaneously, and the option skew on both legs is already paid up for exactly that outcome.

market_context.valuation_assessment: The two dossiers independently generate the same bilateral valuation reading. Canada's BIS real broad effective exchange rate is 95.71 (June 2026) against Switzerland's 101.69, making the Canadian dollar 5.88% cheaper in real trade-weighted terms; applied to spot, that implies a CAD/CHF reference level of approximately 0.6100. Spot at 0.57412 is therefore 6.1% below relative-REER parity, and full convergence would require the pair to clear its 52-week high of 0.60047. Canada's real rate has fallen in eleven of thirteen months to the lowest print in its series and sits near a decade low, while Switzerland's has fallen only 2.5% from its February peak to the 40th percentile of its window — Canada is genuinely cheap and Switzerland is merely fair, which is the configuration in which a positive-carry cross has valuation running with it. This should be read as a relative-REER proxy rather than an absolute PPP estimate, and it is a strategic signal: a 6.1% real gap does not close inside four weeks.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since May has been a low-volatility, positive-carry grind in which CAD/CHF has repeatedly attempted and failed to escape a 0.5645–0.5823 band. The proximate driver has been a global monetary regime shift that hurt the franc more than it helped the loonie: the ECB, BoJ and RBNZ all hiked in June–July, MAS tightened twice, three FOMC voters dissented for a hike, and the SNB alone published a forecast conditioned on zero for three more years, with the market explicitly re-designating the franc as the world's cheapest funding leg, displacing the yen. Against that, the Canadian dollar spent July failing to monetise a 31% Brent rally because the oil shock lifted US term premium rather than Canadian yields, and it now carries a dated, unpriced 19 August tariff cliff.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Annualised carry is +225bp in favour of a long CAD/CHF position (BoC 2.25% vs SNB 0.00%), widening at every point on the curve to +271bp at 2Y and +311bp at 10Y. Measured on money-market fixings the gap is slightly wider at +235bp (CORRA 2.31% vs SARON -0.04%). Using estimated 3M implied vol of 6.0–6.3%, the carry-to-vol ratio is +0.36 to +0.38, among the best risk-adjusted carry available to a Canadian dollar long anywhere in the G10, behind only AUD/CHF and roughly level with NZD/CHF. Every marker of a functioning carry environment is present: VIX 17.09, IG OAS 80bp, HY OAS 284bp, S&P 500 at 7,489.72, and pair realised vol of 5.1%. The distinguishing feature of CAD/CHF versus other franc-funded expressions is that its target leg is not a high-beta growth currency at a stretched valuation — Canada's REER is near a decade low, which is why the pair has lagged rather than a reason to avoid it. The forward curve does nothing but restate the interest differential and contains no view whatsoever, so our expected path runs against it at every tenor and the two return sources compound.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: A +225bp policy differential widening to +271bp at 2Y and +311bp at 10Y, between the two most policy-static central banks in the G10. This pair qualifies for the framework's high-carry boost and the differential's reliability — neither bank meets in the tactical window and the SNB has pre-committed to zero through 2028 — makes it the most dependable single input.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is +225bp at the policy rate, +271bp at two years and +311bp at ten years, and every one of those gaps is anchored at the Swiss end by a central bank that has published a conditional inflation forecast of 0.6%/0.6%/0.7% for 2026–2028 explicitly constructed on the assumption that the policy rate remains at 0.00% throughout. The trajectory is flat-to-widening rather than narrowing: the Bank of Canada's own Market Participants Survey has 2.25% held through December 2026 with no hike until March 2027, while the market carries 12–25bp of residual SNB hawkish premium that the SNB's own forecast repudiates — meaning the more likely repricing over four weeks is a decay of Swiss front-end premium, which widens the gap. Pricing is where the bilateral edge sits: the pair trades at the 36th percentile of its 52-week range and 6.1% below relative-REER parity while earning a 225bp differential, which is a market that has priced the base leg's tariff risk and the quote leg's structural surplus but not the carry. The transmission mechanism is direct and mechanical: with no interbank depth of its own, CAD/CHF is the arithmetic quotient of USD/CHF over USD/CAD, and the Swiss leg of that quotient is the more responsive to global rate moves because the franc is now the marginal funding currency. Critically for the tactical window, neither central bank meets: the BoC next decides on 2 September and the SNB on 24 September, so the differential is a fixed parameter for the entire horizon and the only live risk is a third-party rate shock. That is precisely why this is the highest-confidence factor in the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential is more likely to widen than to narrow, and the asymmetry is dated. On the Canadian side, the 28 October Monetary Policy Report was built on the oil futures curve of 9 July and assumes Brent near $75 in Q3-2026 settling to $70 with WTI stabilising at $65, against actual WTI of $84.25 and Brent of $91.82 — a $19–20 error in the inflationary direction, sitting behind Governing Council's published commitment that a sustained oil increase with broadening spillovers would likely require a monetary policy response. Two of three sell-side houses with live forecasts already carry BoC hikes and the MPS terminal is 2.75%, 50bp above spot policy. On the Swiss side there is no symmetric optionality whatever: the SNB meets only four times a year, has pre-committed to zero in its own forecast through 2028, and source reporting has SNB insiders seeing the policy rate unchanged at 0.00% until the end of 2027. The realistic strategic distribution runs from 225bp (both hold) to 250bp (BoC hikes in December) with only a low-probability path to 200bp. Transmission over this horizon works through the term structure as much as the front end: at +311bp on ten years, Swiss institutional demand for Canadian duration is structurally powerful. Confidence is four points below tactical only because six months contains two SNB assessments and a December Monetary Policy Report, each of which could reprice the Swiss curve if energy-driven inflation broadens.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential has inverted in Canada's favour inside the last four weeks. Canadian real GDP by industry rose 0.3% in May and 0.2% on the June advance estimate, implying roughly +0.8% quarterly expansion in Q2 after 0.0% in Q1 and -0.2% in Q4-2025, while unemployment fell for a second consecutive month to 6.5%, wages accelerated to +3.3% y/y and retail sales hit a record $73.7bn. Switzerland's Q1 GDP was +0.66% q/q and +0.59% y/y on the harmonised basis, unemployment is drifting higher, and the manufacturing PMI fell three points to 54.3 in June. The inflation differential is enormous and structural: Canadian headline CPI 2.8% against Swiss 0.5% is a 230bp gap, and core is 1.8% against 0.3%, a 150bp gap. But the bilateral subtlety neither dossier states is that real policy rates are almost identical — Canada -0.55%, Switzerland -0.50% — so the entire 225bp nominal carry is inflation compensation rather than real yield, which caps how far the fundamental case can be pushed. Transmission is asymmetric: Canadian data moves this pair far more than Swiss data because the BoC is a live reaction function while the SNB is pinned. Three Canadian prints land inside the window — LFS on 7 August, CPI on 17 August, Q2 GDP on 28 August — all carrying upside risk to the pair.

Switzerland's trajectory is a downgrade with a date: Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs at a 15% capped rate hit Switzerland's largest export category to the US, with EY marking 2026 Swiss growth at 0.6% against the SNB's 'around 1%,' and Q2 Swiss real export growth was only +0.6% against +8.8% nominal. The offsetting risk is the inflation channel operating in reverse: Brent at 91.82 is 25% above its year-ago level and has already lifted Swiss headline CPI from 0.1% in February to 0.5% in June; if Swiss headline sustains above 1.0% with core above 0.6%, the SNB regains policy optionality it currently does not have. Symmetrically, if Canadian CPI-trim falls below 1.7% the BoC's hawkish option closes. The realistic central case is Swiss headline drifting to 0.6–0.8% while Canadian core reverts toward 2.0%, leaving the differential broadly intact.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/CHF is a genuine risk-proxy pair by construction — a commodity-linked growth currency against the world's premier safe haven. On the framework's classification it sits between 'pure risk proxy' (AUD/CHF, NZD/CHF) and 'moderate,' because the Canadian dollar's risk beta is structurally lower than the Antipodeans' — roughly 75% of Canadian goods exports go to the United States, so a strong US economy supports Canada through the trade channel even when it hurts through the rate channel. The current regime is unambiguously carry-on and haven-off: VIX 17.09, IG OAS 80bp, HY OAS 284bp, S&P 500 at 7,489.72, and gold down 12.14% over three months and 17.94% over six from its February peak. Gold matters because it shares a debasement-and-uncertainty demand function with the franc, so an 18% gold drawdown is direct evidence the quote leg's structural bid is dormant. The equity-correlation differential runs the pair's way: CAD's correlation to global equities is positive and CHF's is negative. The honest caveat, and the reason confidence is 58 rather than 70, is that the pair has conspicuously failed to monetise this: in a regime with equities near highs, gold down 18% and Brent up 31%, CAD/CHF is flat over twelve months. The risk channel is helping at the margin and being overwhelmed by the base leg's own carry disadvantage to the dollar.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months this factor becomes genuinely two-sided and we score it Neutral rather than force a direction. The bullish limb is that the current low-volatility, tight-credit, AI-capex environment favours a US-linked commodity economy. The bearish limb is that this pair is the G10's most doubly convex loser in a risk event: a genuine shock weakens CAD through the growth and commodity-demand channel and bids CHF through the haven channel simultaneously, so the two legs compound rather than offset. As stock markets tumbled in early August 2024, the Swiss franc jumped as much as 3.5% over two days, and the SNB's removal of its euro peg in 2015 triggered a flash rally that wiped out years of carry trade gains. A 3.5% two-day franc rally combined with a simultaneous 1–2% CAD decline would take CAD/CHF down 450–550 pips — more than three years of carry at 225bp. With high-yield spreads at 284bp against a 3.63% funds rate and equities pricing a benign resolution to a tightening cycle that has barely begun, the six-month distribution is skewed toward deterioration. Both parent dossiers name an equity correction as a principal downside risk. The symmetry of that downside against a merely continuing benign base case is the definition of a Neutral factor at this horizon.

Those roughly cancel in directional terms but they do not cancel in path terms — the distribution becomes fat-tailed on the downside because the franc-funded book unwinds violently.

The crowded side of this cross is demonstrably the bearish side, and the market has almost no capacity left to add to it.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral trade relationship is, unusually, almost irrelevant to this pair and that fact is itself the finding. Per IMF DOTS for 2024, Canadian exports to Switzerland were $4.6bn and imports from Switzerland $5.8bn, giving Canada a net goods deficit of $1.2bn — a rounding error against Canada's $77.1bn record monthly export print. Switzerland reports imports from Canada of $8.5bn against Canada's reported $4.6bn of exports, a $3.9bn discrepancy almost certainly attributable to non-monetary gold transiting Swiss refineries. The practical consequence is that the terms-of-trade channel for CAD/CHF operates entirely through third-party commodity prices. Applying the framework's direction rules: oil ↑ → ++CAD and −CHF, so net pair rises; natural gas ↑ → mildly +CAD and −CHF, net pair rises; gold ↑ → +CHF and mildly +CAD, net pair falls — but gold is down 17.94% over six months, currently pair-bullish. Canada's record $77.1bn monthly exports and $11.6bn bilateral US surplus land against Switzerland's Q2 real export growth of just +0.6%.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.16 strategic weight this is where the two dossiers conflict most sharply. Switzerland runs a current-account surplus of +9.77% of GDP against Canada's -0.87%, a 10.6-percentage-point gap, and Switzerland holds a net international investment position of CHF 974bn as a structural net creditor. Switzerland's surplus is diversified across pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and watches, finance and commodity trading, and a large primary income surplus. That level creates persistent, price-insensitive franc demand that reasserts whenever the cyclical funding-outflow story pauses, and over one to six months the level dominates the change. The change runs the other way — Canada's external accounts are compounding on the oil move — but Switzerland's largest export line now faces a 15% US tariff plus a USD 200bn corporate investment pledge, a multi-year franc-selling capital outflow. Netting honestly: the tariff and pledge might compress the Swiss surplus by 1–2pp of GDP over several years, still more than eight percentage points above Canada's. This is the single largest structural pair-bearish fact in the analysis, and it is why we bound the strategic upside at 0.6050 rather than extrapolating to relative-REER parity.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The guidance divergence between these two central banks is the widest in the G10 and it runs entirely in the pair's favour. The Bank of Canada has published a conditional hawkish trigger — that a sustained oil increase with broadening spillovers would likely require a monetary policy response — reinforced by Governor Macklem's statement that the Bank will not let higher oil prices become persistent inflation. The Swiss National Bank has done the opposite: it has published a three-year conditional inflation forecast built on a flat 0.00% policy rate, with reporting that SNB insiders see the rate unchanged until end-2027. The asymmetry is about optionality: the BoC retains a live reaction function; the SNB has removed itself as a variable. There is a second, one-directional mechanism: the SNB's intervention pledge is explicitly asymmetric, committing to counter rapid franc appreciation and saying nothing about resisting weakness — placing an official-sector cap on CAD/CHF downside and no cap on its upside. Sequencing also favours the base leg: the BoC decides 2 September, the SNB not until 24 September, so Canada sets the tone.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.12 strategic weight this becomes the pair's second-largest positive contributor, and the strategic case is stronger than the tactical one because it hinges on dated events. The 28 October Monetary Policy Report is the mechanism: it was built on a stale oil futures curve and assumes currency weakness already, meaning any appreciation is a disinflationary surprise. The Bank must raise its oil path, mechanically lifting its inflation profile and confronting Governing Council with its own published trigger; a credible institution does not publish that sentence and then ignore oil sitting $20 above its assumption. Partially offsetting, the same MPR must cut its growth forecast for Section 338. On the quote side there is no comparable mechanism: ING's forecast is the SNB on hold throughout 2027, and it identifies this as a factor driving Swiss franc underperformance when global rates rise on higher oil prices. That is the pair thesis stated by a third party. The credibility differential is genuine but symmetric — both institutions have excellent records — so the strategic edge rests on optionality, and the SNB has none. The residual risk is the SNB's own history of discontinuity.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral event landscape has a symmetry that neither dossier can see from its own side: both currencies face dated US trade action, and the two partially cancel. On the base leg, three presidential proclamations signed 20 July impose 50% Section 338 tariffs on Canadian motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages and dairy — roughly $20bn of trade — effective around 19 August, applying regardless of USMCA origin, with no Canadian retaliation announced. On the quote leg, Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs at a 15% capped rate for Switzerland took effect 31 July for Annex III companies and extend to all other importers on 29 September. The relative magnitudes decide the net: Canada's measure carries a punitive 50% rate on a broad consumer-goods base with no USMCA shelter, against an economy sending roughly 75% of its goods exports to the US; Switzerland's was negotiated down from a 39% headline in exchange for a USD 200bn investment pledge and is competitively advantageous relative to uncapped jurisdictions. Net: the trade-policy channel is pair-bearish tactically, because the Canadian measure is larger, closer, and demonstrably unpriced. The Hormuz channel is genuinely ambiguous — escalation is pair-bullish through oil and pair-bearish through the haven bid, and the haven channel historically dominates on impact while oil dominates on persistence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two trade shocks converge toward equivalence and the factor nets to Neutral. Canada's position is genuinely open-ended — the USMCA was not renewed and remains in force pending resolution, a persistent risk premium — but the precedent for reversal is strong given the February 2026 IEEPA termination. Switzerland's shock is fully quantified and capped but extends economy-wide on 29 September, and its associated USD 200bn corporate investment pledge is a multi-year, structural franc-selling capital outflow that will not reverse and is pair-bullish throughout. Domestic political risk is negligible on both sides. One structural tail deserves naming: Swiss banking concentration post-2023 means any UBS-specific stress would be systemic for the quote leg and would produce a franc sell-off rather than a haven bid — a pair-bullish tail with no Canadian analogue. Netting a possibly-reversible base-leg negative against a certain-but-capped quote-leg negative plus a structural outflow gives no directional signal at a 0.05 weight.

Spot at 0.57412 is above the 50-day (0.57298), 100-day (0.57183) and 200-day (0.57123), correctly stacked — nominally bullish. Realised vol of 5.1% against a proxy 3M implied of 6.0–6.71% implies a positive variance risk premium of roughly 1.0–1.2 vol points, the reverse of both parent dossiers. Liquidity is the structural caveat: this is an intermediated cross with no native interbank depth, warranting attention specifically in New York and London sessions.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/CHF has no USD leg, so this factor transmits indirectly — but for this specific cross the indirect channel is unusually strong. Ample dollar liquidity is the precondition for scalable carry, and the franc is now the marginal funding currency for that carry, so easy dollar conditions translate mechanically into franc supply. The current backdrop is clean: SOFR fixed at 3.65% exactly at IORB, the Fed's balance sheet stood at $6.738tn having grown roughly $109bn since early March, QT ended 1 December 2025 and the Desk is purchasing Treasury bills. There is no funding stress to force deleveraging of franc-funded positions. The second, more specific channel is a relative dollar beta asymmetry appearing in neither dossier as a pair statement: over six months USD/CHF rose 4.64% while USD/CAD rose only 2.16%, meaning the franc has roughly twice the sensitivity of the loonie to a firming dollar. Consequently a strong-dollar regime has been pair-bullish, counter-intuitive for a cross with no dollar leg. Both parent dossiers flag that cross-currency basis data was unobtainable, so the assessment rests on SOFR-IORB and the absence of reported stress.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the balance-sheet channel becomes the dominant transmission and it remains pair-bullish, though at reduced confidence. A Fed that has ended runoff and begun purchasing Treasury bills is adding to global dollar supply, which has historically weighed on the dollar with a two-to-four-quarter lag. For CAD/CHF the consequence is two-sided: a softer dollar removes the relative-beta tailwind, but it also historically coincides with stronger commodity prices and firmer global growth, favouring the base leg. The franc's funding-currency status is more durable, resting on the SNB expected at zero into 2027 versus a BoJ heading toward 1.25% with demonstrated intervention willingness. Two identified strategic risks run the other way: December year-end cross-currency basis seasonality, where basis conventionally widens as bank balance sheets are constrained exactly when liquidity is thinnest; and reserve adequacy, where approaching the Fed's minimum comfortable level would tighten money markets and transmit to franc-funded positions immediately.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.525 on a -1.00 to +1.00 scale is a firmly bullish reading for CAD/CHF, and the construction is unusually clean: seven of ten factors are Bullish, two are Neutral (contributing exactly zero rather than offsetting), and only one — Event Risk at -0.0275 — is negative. Policy & Rates alone contributes +0.1998, and Policy plus Inflation & Growth plus Risk Appetite account for +0.3712, or 71% of the total.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights this pair is dominated by Policy & Rates (0.27), Inflation & Growth (0.16) and Risk Appetite (0.13), which together carry 56% of the weight and all three point the same way for CAD/CHF rising. The reason they align is mechanical rather than narrative: the Bank of Canada sits at 2.25% against a Swiss National Bank at 0.00%, the gap widens to +271bp at two years and +311bp at ten, and neither central bank meets inside the four-week window — so the differential is a fixed parameter for the entire horizon and the only live risk to it is a third-party rate shock. That produces a net weighted score of +0.525 with seven Bullish factors and a single small negative, which is a bullish result generated by signal rather than by netting opposing views. The base and quote dossier views are genuinely reinforcing here, and asymmetrically so: the CAD dossier is Neutral tactically at conviction 2 while the CHF dossier is Bearish at conviction 4, so the pair inherits most of its direction from the quote leg — a franc that has been reassigned from haven to the world's cheapest funding currency and whose central bank has published a three-year forecast conditioned on doing nothing. Three bilateral factors materially modify the standalone views. First, positioning: netting a 99th-percentile CAD short against a 28th-percentile CHF short leaves the market implicitly short CAD/CHF by roughly USD 7.4bn with the squeeze fuel concentrated entirely in the base leg — a signal that exists in neither dossier and that gives the pair an upside asymmetry into three dated Canadian data events. Second, trade policy: Canada's 50% Section 338 tariffs on ~$20bn from 19 August are partially offset bilaterally by Switzerland's 15% capped Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs extending 29 September, which is why the largest negative in the CAD dossier shrinks to a -0.0275 contribution here. Third, dollar beta: USD/CHF has risen 4.64% over six months against USD/CAD's 2.16%, meaning the franc carries roughly twice the loonie's sensitivity to a firming dollar and a strong-dollar regime is therefore pair-bullish — counter-intuitive for a cross with no dollar leg and unavailable from either standalone view. What is priced against what we expect is the edge: the one-month forward outright is 0.57298, a -11.4 point discount that is nothing but the interest differential, while spot sits at the 36th percentile of its 52-week range and 6.1% below relative-REER parity of 0.6100 — a market that has priced both currencies' risks and neither's carry. The path of least resistance is a grind toward the 0.5790–0.5820 shelf, though the 17.5-pip moving-average cluster means no trend flow will assist it and the move should be news-driven rather than momentum-driven. The dated catalysts are dense and mostly base-leg: Canadian LFS 7 August, the August EIA STEO 11 August, Canadian CPI 17 August, Section 338 effective ~19 August, Canadian Q2 GDP 28 August, BoC 2 September. Conviction is 4 rather than 5 because the distribution is not symmetric around the central case in the way the score implies — this pair loses on both legs simultaneously in a risk event, on a historical template worth 450–550 pips or more than three years of carry, and the option skew on both legs is already paid up for exactly that outcome.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among the nine Canadian dollar crosses, CAD/CHF ranks 2nd most attractive long, behind only CAD/JPY, which combines +125bp of carry with a doubly asymmetric oil channel and a yen REER at the third percentile against Switzerland's 40th. It beats every other CAD cross on risk-adjusted terms: CAD/CHF delivers Canada's best carry-to-vol ratio anywhere in the G10 at roughly +0.30 to +0.38, against negative ratios versus USD, GBP, AUD and NOK, and only +0.06 versus SEK and 0.00 versus EUR. Among the ten Swiss franc crosses, CAD/CHF ranks 4th most attractive franc short, behind USD/CHF (363bp), AUD/CHF (435bp, though against a 97th-percentile Australian real exchange rate) and NZD/CHF (250bp, fastest-widening differential of any peer). The uncomfortable comparison is USD/CHF, which earns 138bp more carry with a cleaner catalyst calendar; the uncomfortable comparison in the other direction is that the CHF dossier's own relative-value list names long CHF/CAD as its purest franc-bullish expression, which we disagree with and consider the honest statement of where this trade's risk lies. Across the full G10 opportunity set, CAD/CHF sits in the top quintile of roughly 45 major crosses on a carry-plus-valuation screen and the second quintile on conviction.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.300 is a moderately bullish reading — 43% smaller than the tactical +0.525 — driven by Policy & Rates (+0.1890), Guidance (+0.0792), Inflation & Growth (+0.0550) and USD Liquidity (+0.0416), offset by a single large negative: External Balance at -0.0800, whose weight nearly triples strategically and whose stance flips from Bullish to Bearish. strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the framework redistributes materially and the redistribution costs the pair roughly 22 points of score: External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16 with its stance flipping from Bullish to Bearish (a swing of -0.115), Guidance rises from 0.07 to 0.12 with its stance intact (+0.036), Inflation & Growth falls from 0.16 to 0.10 (-0.041), Risk Appetite falls from 0.13 to 0.07 and turns Neutral (-0.075), and the base-leg positioning contribution disappears entirely (-0.064). Policy & Rates still dominates and still points up: the differential is +225bp today, widens to +271bp at two years and +311bp at ten, and the realistic six-month distribution runs from 225bp to 250bp with only a low-probability path to 200bp, because the Bank of Canada has a published conditional hawkish trigger and a stale oil assumption while the Swiss National Bank has pre-committed to zero through 2028. Guidance reinforces that with a date: the 28 October Monetary Policy Report must raise an oil path that is $19 wrong in the inflationary direction, against Governing Council's own statement that such a scenario would likely require a monetary policy response, and there is no comparable Swiss mechanism because the SNB is not revising anything before 10 December. Those two factors interact, and the interaction is the strategic thesis: it is guidance, not the rate level itself, that converted the franc from a cyclical low-yielder into the world's structural funding currency, and third-party analysis has stated the transmission directly. The conflicting input is Switzerland's external position, and it is genuine rather than decorative: a 10.6-percentage-point current-account gap and a CHF 974bn creditor stock create persistent, price-insensitive franc demand that reasserts whenever the funding-outflow story pauses, and it is why the pair has gone nowhere for a year despite a 225bp carry. What is priced versus what we expect is the clearest edge in the dossier: the six-month forward outright is 0.56732, embedding a 2.37% pair depreciation that is nothing but the interest differential, while relative-REER parity sits 6.1% above spot at 0.6100 — so the forward is paying us to hold a pair the real exchange rate says is cheap. Our expected six-month spot is 0.5900, a 227-pip edge to the forward. The path of least resistance is a stepped grind punctuated by the central-bank calendar, with the inflection at the 28 October MPR. The dated catalysts that matter are 24 September, 29 September, 28 October, 9 December and the December year-end basis turn. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the single largest strategic negative is also the single most heavily weighted factor after rates, and because the base case requires clearing a shelf that has failed twice.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically CAD/CHF improves to 1st among Canadian dollar crosses, overtaking CAD/JPY, because the strategic framework rewards exactly what this cross has and penalises what CAD/JPY has: the yen's real effective exchange rate at the third percentile is the most undervalued in the G10 and the BoJ is normalising toward 1.25%, so CAD/JPY's carry engine is losing thrust and its valuation runway is against it. CAD/CHF has the opposite configuration: Canada is 5.88% cheap to Switzerland on relative REER, and the SNB loses nothing to normalisation because it is not normalising. It also beats short AUD/CAD and short EUR/CAD. Among the ten franc crosses, CAD/CHF holds at 4th strategically, still behind USD/CHF, AUD/CHF and NZD/CHF on raw carry but ahead of them on the quality of the target leg: Australia's real exchange rate at the 97th percentile and New Zealand's 4.06% inflation are both cyclical peaks, whereas Canada's REER near a decade low and its 0.7%-to-1.8% growth acceleration are cyclical troughs. Across the full G10 opportunity set the pair sits in the second quintile strategically. The direct disagreement remains worth naming: the CHF dossier's own relative-value framework recommends short CAD/CHF as its purest franc-bullish expression, and we take the other side.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The two horizons share an identical reading of the facts and differ almost entirely in what the framework pays for. cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The highest-quality part of the expected return is concentrated in the tactical window and in the two months following the October MPR, not evenly across six months. CAD gross longs stand at only 26,391 against a gross short of 128,886, mechanically amplifying the reaction to a beat.

June printed +0.5% headline with core at 0.3%, and July faces an unfavourable energy base effect as the March–April Brent spike drops out. A print at or below 0.3% would revive negative-rate speculation and collapse the residual SNB hawkish premium, pair-bullish; a print above 0.8% with core above 0.5% would restore quote-leg optionality, pair-bearish. The skew favours the pair because the base effect points down.

The July issue was finalised before the Hormuz re-escalation, forecasting Brent at $74 in Q3-2026 and $65 in 2027 — roughly $18 below spot. An upward revision is doubly transmitting for this cross: oil up is ++CAD for the world's fourth-largest crude exporter and -CHF for an economy with no domestic hydrocarbon production, so the two legs move in opposite directions and the pair captures both.

The pivotal base-leg print and genuinely two-sided. June headline fell to 2.8% while CPI-trim fell to 1.8% and CPI-median to 1.9%, both below target. A reversal in the cores above 2.0% revives the BoC hawkish option, widening the differential toward 250bp and is pair-bullish; a further decline toward 1.7% forecloses it for 2026 and is pair-bearish.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement
catalysts.rationale: A hold at 2.25% is near-certain; the information is entirely in whether Governing Council maintains the pure look-through framing on oil or begins to lean on the conditional trigger it published on 29 July. Sequencing matters bilaterally: the BoC speaks three weeks before the SNB, setting the tone for the differential.

Q1 was +0.4% q/q sport-adjusted, and Q2 is the first quarter to capture the full trade-uncertainty effect preceding the pharmaceutical tariff, with Q2 real export growth of only +0.6% against +8.8% nominal. A print below 0.2% would confirm EY's 0.6% annual estimate over the SNB's 'around 1%' and is pair-bullish through the quote leg's growth channel, though Swiss weakness does not translate into SNB action since it is already at zero.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: The largest third-party event in the window, transmitting through the relative dollar beta rather than directly. Over six months USD/CHF rose 4.64% against USD/CAD's 2.16%, meaning the franc carries roughly twice the loonie's sensitivity to a firming dollar — so a hawkish SEP is pair-bullish even though it hurts both legs against the dollar.

catalysts.event: SNB Monetary Policy Assessment and news conference
catalysts.rationale: The single largest scheduled quote-leg event of the horizon and the pair's secondary inflection point. The SNB revises its conditional inflation forecast for the first time since the energy shock re-intensified. An upward revision above 0.9% for 2027 validates the market's residual hawkish premium and is pair-bearish; a downward revision toward 0.4% revives negative-rate speculation and is pair-bullish.

catalysts.event: US Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs extend to all non-Annex-III Swiss importers
catalysts.rationale: The 15% capped rate becomes economy-wide rather than concentrated in the seventeen largest firms, striking Switzerland's largest export category to the US. This is the bilateral counterweight to the base leg's 19 August tariff and it is what reduces the pair's net event-risk exposure to a -0.0275 tactical contribution.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision and Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: The designated inflection point for the strategic thesis. The July MPR assumes Brent near $75 and WTI at $65 against actual levels of $91.82 and $84.25. The Bank must raise its oil path, lifting its inflation profile and confronting Governing Council with its own published trigger, with no corresponding Swiss revision until 10 December.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement (final 2026 decision)
catalysts.rationale: The meeting at which any October MPR revision translates into action or explicit signalling. A hike or hawkish signal would take the differential to 250bp against a quote leg with no path off zero, and would compress the CA–CH two-year spread beyond 290bp — the single largest available strategic repricing for the pair.

catalysts.rationale: The SNB's most information-rich event of the year, falling one day after the BoC's final decision — an unusually tight clustering that could amplify or cancel. It is also immediately before the December year-end cross-currency basis turn, compounding volatility for franc-funded positions.

Basis conventionally widens into year-end as bank balance sheets are constrained, raising the cost of franc-funded positions precisely when liquidity is thinnest. For a pair whose quote leg is the market's designated global funding currency, this is a mechanical, dated funding-cost shock rather than a thesis event, expected to produce a sharp 1–2% counter-trend decline that should be faded rather than followed.

This is the pair's most dangerous single variable because CAD/CHF is the G10's clearest example of a cross where a volatility shock hits both legs in the same direction. For USD/CHF a VIX spike is one-sided; for CAD/JPY it is partially offset by oil; for CAD/CHF it compounds.

Oil is the only variable that moves both legs of this pair in opposite directions, doubling its transmission relative to any single-currency view. A $10 move is worth roughly 0.8–1.2% on the pair, materially more than its effect on either currency's trade-weighted index.

assumptions: Pair convention: all stances are expressed in CAD/CHF terms; Bullish means the pair rises, Bearish means it falls. This inverts the base dossier's convention, which expresses CAD views as USD/CAD falling.

Spot, the 52-week range, range percentile, moving averages, trend regime, recent price-action narrative and realised-volatility estimate are taken from the provided 390-day Twelve Data OHLC series. The pre-calculated performance figures (1M -0.26%, 3M +1.42%, 6M -0.02%, 1Y +0.01%) do not reconcile exactly to simple calendar look-backs on the same OHLC series and are reported as supplied per the data-source rule.

Support and resistance, chart patterns and technical consensus are taken exclusively from web research, as visual chart analysis is not derivable from raw OHLC; sources disagree materially, which is reported as a finding rather than resolved by preference.

No CAD/CHF volatility surface exists in accessible data. Realised volatility of approximately 5.1% annualised is computed from provided daily closes and may be biased downward by non-trading-day entries; 5.5–6.0% is a more realistic range. The 3M implied estimate of 6.0–6.71% is bracketed by a zero-correlation proxy at the top and the realised estimate at the bottom; all carry-to-vol ratios should be read as rank orderings rather than precise levels.

Forward points are computed via covered interest parity on the 235bp money-market differential, not observed; no CAD/CHF forward quotes were obtainable and cross-currency basis for both legs was unobtainable, so computed points do not incorporate any basis adjustment.

Valuation is a relative-REER proxy (Canada's BIS real broad REER 95.71 versus Switzerland's 101.69), not an absolute PPP calculation, and should be read as an ordinal cheapness measure rather than a forecast or target.

Bilateral trade is taken directly from the supplied IMF DOTS block for 2024; the $3.9bn mirror discrepancy is interpreted as non-monetary gold transiting Swiss refineries, an inference rather than a sourced statement.

Consensus for this pair is weak evidence: no major bank publishes a CAD/CHF forecast; the retail-model cluster is drawn from algorithmic sites with proprietary methodologies, several anchored to stale spot levels; the bank-derived cross is an arithmetic construction, not a forecast any institution has made.
Weight adjustments are documented with specific bilateral reasons, all within the ±0.05 per-factor limit, and both columns sum to exactly 1.00.

Scoring methodology: stance scores are Bullish +1, Neutral 0, Bearish -1, multiplied by confidence/100 and by horizon weight; conviction mapped from absolute net score using bands below 0.10=1, 0.10-0.20=2, 0.20-0.35=3, 0.35-0.55=4, above 0.55=5.

Scenario probabilities (50/25/25 base/upside/downside) are subjective and follow the framework's standard structure; individual invalidator probabilities are independent estimates and do not sum to 100% since conditions are not mutually exclusive.

All policy rates, sovereign yields, CFTC positioning, current-account ratios, CPI/GDP figures, central-bank language, tariff details and BIS REER levels are drawn from the two supplied dossiers and carry their own citation trails and flags, including unretrievable volatility surfaces and cross-currency basis on both legs.
